Link Rot and Content Drift in Academic Citations

Link rot is the process by which hyperlinks stop pointing to the resources they originally referenced. In a study of academic citations, researchers followed thousands of URLs cited in scholarly journals between 1996 and 2019. They found that a large share of the cited web pages were no longer reachable, and that many more still loaded but no longer contained the material the authors had cited, a problem the authors call content drift.

The study measured decay by checking each URL against snapshots in the Internet Archive. Links in law reviews decayed faster than links in medical journals, and links to personal homepages decayed fastest of all. The authors recommend that publishers archive every cited page at the time of citation, and that readers check the Wayback Machine when a citation fails.

Content drift is harder to detect than outright failure because the page still returns a normal response. Automated link checkers report these links as healthy even though the cited evidence has disappeared. The authors propose comparing the cited version with the current version of each page.

Update 2024: a follow-up study confirmed these findings for citations published after 2019, and several publishers now archive cited pages automatically.
